note: Two independent blind passes agreed on all 100 letters (crosstab: AGREE 100, DISPUTE 0, TWIN 0), so nothing required reconciliation between them. This paper has NO answer key of any kind. Items flagged MED/LOW carry an adjudication note on the row; where no printed option is correct the row says so explicitly rather than presenting the best reading as a verified answer.

derivations.reasoning: Remainder mod a quadratic is linear: r(x)=ax+b. p(1)=2 gives a+b=2; p(2)=1 gives 2a+b=1. So a=-1, b=3 and r(x)=3-x.
For x>0, AM-GM gives x+1/x >= 2. Hence x+1/x > 1 (I true), (x+1/x)^2 >= 4 > 2 (II true), (x+1/x)^4 >= 16 > 9 (III true). All three hold.
derivations.solution: For every \(x>0\), AM-GM gives \(x+\dfrac{1}{x}\ge 2\). Hence \(x+\dfrac{1}{x}>1\), \(\left(x+\dfrac{1}{x}\right)^{2}\ge 4>2\) and \(\left(x+\dfrac{1}{x}\right)^{4}\ge 16>9\), so all three statements are correct.

derivations.reasoning: AS PRINTED the expression is q^2-5p-4 while the question asks for the largest p, so p and q are mixed. Taking the only sensible reading (there exists a natural q>p making it negative), the smallest admissible q is p+1, so (p+1)^2 < 5p+4, i.e. p^2-3p-3<0, i.e. p < (3+sqrt21)/2 = 3.79, giving p=3 (checked: p=3,q=4 gives 16-15-4=-3<0; p=4,q=5 gives 25-20-4=+1). Verified by brute force. RUNNER-UP C (5): if the stem were meant to read p^2-5p-4<0 the answer is p=5, and the option set (3,4,5,6) is consistent with that intent. C wins only if the printed q^2 is a misprint for p^2.
derivations.solution: As printed the expression mixes the two letters — it reads \(q^{2}-5p-4\) while the question asks for the largest \(p\) — so it has to be taken as: the largest \(p\) for which some natural \(q>p\) makes it negative. The best chance is the smallest such \(q\), namely \(q=p+1\), which needs \((p+1)^{2}<5p+4\), i.e. \(p^{2}-3p-3<0\) and so \(p<\dfrac{3+\sqrt{21}}{2}\approx 3.79\). Checking, \(p=3,\ q=4\) gives \(16-15-4=-3<0\) while \(p=4,\ q=5\) gives \(25-20-4=+1\), so the largest value is \(p=3\). Had the printed \(q^{2}\) been a misprint for \(p^{2}\), the same working would have given 5 instead.

derivations.reasoning: x-y prime forces x>y. If both x,y were odd primes then x+y and x-y are both even, and both cannot be 2. So y=2, x an odd prime with x-2 and x+2 both prime: only x=5 (3,5,7) below 20. Exhaustive search over x,y<20 returns exactly one quadruple (5,2,7,3).
derivations.solution: Since \(x-y\) must itself be prime it is positive, so \(x>y\). If \(x\) and \(y\) were both odd primes then \(x+y\) and \(x-y\) would both be even, and they cannot both equal 2 — so \(y=2\). That leaves an odd prime \(x\) with \(x-2\) and \(x+2\) also prime, and below 20 the only such value is \(x=5\), giving the primes 3, 5 and 7. Exactly one combination is possible, namely \((5,\ 2,\ 7,\ 3)\).

derivations.reasoning: x^4-1=(x-1)(x+1)(x^2+1), so (x+p)(x^2+p^2) must be (x-1)(x^2+1), giving p=-1. Sympy coefficient matching returns p=-1 uniquely.
derivations.solution: Factorise the right-hand side as \(x^{4}-1=(x-1)(x+1)(x^{2}+1)\). Cancelling the common factor \((x+1)\) leaves \((x+p)(x^{2}+p^{2})=(x-1)(x^{2}+1)\), and comparing the two sides gives \(p=-1\).

derivations.reasoning: (2+sqrt3)(2-sqrt3)=1, so with t=(2+sqrt3)^x the second term is 1/t. t+1/t=2 forces (t-1)^2=0, t=1, x=0. Then the difference is 1-1=0.
derivations.solution: Since \((2+\sqrt{3})(2-\sqrt{3})=4-3=1\), writing \(t=(2+\sqrt{3})^{x}\) makes the second term \(\dfrac{1}{t}\). Then \(t+\dfrac{1}{t}=2\) forces \((t-1)^{2}=0\), so \(t=1\) and \(x=0\). Both terms are therefore 1 and their difference is 0.
Working modulo \(x^{2}+1\) we may replace \(x^{2}\) by \(-1\), so \(x^{6}=(x^{2})^{3}=(-1)^{3}=-1\). The remainder is the constant \(-1\).

derivations.reasoning: (x+2) is a factor iff the polynomial vanishes at x=-2. Evaluated: A -> 0, B -> 128, C -> -48, D -> -56. Only A.
17 = -1 and 19 = 1 (mod 18), so 17^25+19^25 = (-1)^25 + 1 = 0 (mod 18). Direct computation of the integer confirms remainder 0.
derivations.solution: Modulo 18 we have \(17\equiv -1\) and \(19\equiv 1\). Hence \(17^{25}+19^{25}\equiv (-1)^{25}+1^{25}=-1+1=0 \pmod{18}\), so the remainder is 0.

derivations.reasoning: p=(x^3+y^3)/(x^2-xy+y^2)=x+y and q=(x^3-y^3)/(x^2+xy+y^2)=x-y. Writing x=Ha, y=Hb with gcd(a,b)=1, HCF(p,q)=H*gcd(a+b,a-b), and gcd(a+b,a-b) is 1 or 2 (2 exactly when a,b are both odd). Both occur: x=2,y=1 gives H; x=3,y=1 gives 2H.
With u=x^2, u^2=u+1 so u=(1+sqrt5)/2 and x^4=u^2=u+1=(3+sqrt5)/2. Hence 2x^4=3+sqrt5. Sympy gives 2x^4 = sqrt(5)+3 for the positive root.
derivations.solution: Put \(u=x^{2}\); the equation becomes \(u^{2}=u+1\), whose positive root is \(u=\dfrac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\). Then \(x^{4}=u^{2}=u+1=\dfrac{3+\sqrt{5}}{2}\), so \(2x^{4}=3+\sqrt{5}\).

derivations.reasoning: Cross-multiplying and factoring gives (p-r)(p+q+r+s)=0 (sympy factor: -(-p+r)(p+q+r+s)). So either p=r or the sum is zero.
derivations.solution: Cross-multiplying gives \((p+q)(s+p)=(q+r)(r+s)\), which rearranges to \(p^{2}-r^{2}+q(p-r)+s(p-r)=0\). That factorises as \((p-r)(p+q+r+s)=0\), so either \(p=r\) or \(p+q+r+s=0\). Both alternatives genuinely occur, so the combined statement is the correct one rather than either half on its own.

derivations.reasoning: 8n+1 is odd, so gcd(12n+2, 8n+1) = gcd(6n+1, 8n+1) = gcd(6n+1, 2n) = gcd(6n+1, n) = 1 for every n. Checked n=1..6: all gcds equal 1, so all 6 values qualify.

x^3+y^3+3xy-1 = x^3+y^3+(-1)^3-3xy(-1) = (x+y-1)(x^2+y^2+1-xy+x+y). And (x+y)^4-1 = (x+y-1)(x+y+1)((x+y)^2+1). Sympy factorisations confirm the only common factor is (x+y-1); the cofactors are coprime.
derivations.solution: Write the first polynomial as \(x^{3}+y^{3}+(-1)^{3}-3xy(-1)\), which by the standard identity factorises as \((x+y-1)\left(x^{2}+y^{2}+1-xy+x+y\right)\). The second factorises as \((x+y)^{4}-1=(x+y-1)(x+y+1)\left((x+y)^{2}+1\right)\). The remaining cofactors have no common factor, so the HCF is \(x+y-1\).

derivations.reasoning: n even: n=2 gives x=24, not divisible by 48, so I is false (also fails at n=4,10,12). For II, n and n+2 are both even so 8 | x, and one of three consecutive numbers is a multiple of 3, so 24 | x and x^2 is divisible by 576, hence by 144. Checked n=2..18.

Factors: x^4+x^2y^2+y^4=(x^2+xy+y^2)(x^2-xy+y^2); x^3y+y^4=y(x+y)(x^2-xy+y^2); x^4y^2-x^3y^3=x^3y^2(x-y). Sympy LCM = x^3 y^2 (x-y)(x+y)(x^2-xy+y^2)(x^2+xy+y^2) = x^3y^2(x^6-y^6) (difference verified zero).
derivations.solution: Factorise each expression: \(x^{4}+x^{2}y^{2}+y^{4}=(x^{2}+xy+y^{2})(x^{2}-xy+y^{2})\), \(x^{3}y+y^{4}=y(x+y)(x^{2}-xy+y^{2})\) and \(x^{4}y^{2}-x^{3}y^{3}=x^{3}y^{2}(x-y)\). The LCM takes the highest power of every factor, giving \(x^{3}y^{2}(x-y)(x+y)(x^{2}-xy+y^{2})(x^{2}+xy+y^{2})\), which collapses to \(x^{3}y^{2}\left(x^{6}-y^{6}\right)\).

derivations.reasoning: XYZ - ZYX = (100X+10Y+Z)-(100Z+10Y+X) = 99(X-Z), an exact multiple of 99, so the remainder is 0.
Need s^s divisible by 2^9 with s=p+q. s=2 gives 2^2, s=4 gives 2^8 (one short), s=6 gives 2^6*3^6. s=8 gives 2^24. Brute force over s=2..19 returns least s = 8.
derivations.solution: Since \(512=2^{9}\), we need \(s^{s}\) to carry at least nine factors of 2, where \(s=p+q\). An odd \(s\) carries none; \(s=2\) gives \(2^{2}\), \(s=4\) gives \(4^{4}=2^{8}\) — one factor short — and \(s=6\) gives \(6^{6}=2^{6}\cdot 3^{6}\). The first value that works is \(s=8\), since \(8^{8}=2^{24}\).

derivations.reasoning: c^2+bc-a^2-ab=(c-a)(c+a+b), so the first two terms combine to (a+b)(a+b+c)/[(c-a)(c+a+b)] = (a+b)/(c-a). Then (a+b)/(c-a) - (a+2b+c)/(2(c-a)) = (a-c)/(2(c-a)) = -1/2. Sympy simplify returns -1/2.
derivations.solution: The second denominator factorises as \(c^{2}+bc-a^{2}-ab=(c-a)(a+b+c)\). The first two terms then combine to \(\dfrac{(a+b)^{2}+(a+b)c}{(c-a)(a+b+c)}=\dfrac{(a+b)(a+b+c)}{(c-a)(a+b+c)}=\dfrac{a+b}{c-a}\). Subtracting the third term leaves \(\dfrac{2(a+b)-(a+2b+c)}{2(c-a)}=\dfrac{a-c}{2(c-a)}=-\dfrac{1}{2}\).

derivations.reasoning: From a^b=b^a, b^(a/b)=(b^a)^(1/b)=(a^b)^(1/b)=a. The expression is a*(a/b)^(a/b)/a^(a/b) = a/b^(a/b) = a/a = 1. Checked numerically with (a,b)=(2,4) and (4,2): both give 1.
derivations.solution: Split the numerator using \(\left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right)^{a/b}=\dfrac{a^{a/b}}{b^{a/b}}\); the whole expression then reduces to \(\dfrac{a}{b^{a/b}}\). The given condition supplies the rest: \(b^{a/b}=\left(b^{a}\right)^{1/b}=\left(a^{b}\right)^{1/b}=a\). The value is therefore \(\dfrac{a}{a}=1\).

derivations.reasoning: x = 2 + sqrt2 + 2sqrt2 = 2+3sqrt2, x^2 = 22+12sqrt2, so x^2-4x-10 = 22+12sqrt2-8-12sqrt2-10 = 4. Sympy simplify gives 4.
Rationalising gives (p+sqrt(p^2-x^2))/x = p, so sqrt(p^2-x^2)=p(x-1); squaring gives x(p^2+1)=2p^2 (rejecting x=0). Sympy solve returns x = 2p^2/(p^2+1).
derivations.solution: Multiply numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{p+x}+\sqrt{p-x}\): the top becomes \(2p+2\sqrt{p^{2}-x^{2}}\) and the bottom \(2x\), so the condition reads \(\dfrac{p+\sqrt{p^{2}-x^{2}}}{x}=p\). Hence \(\sqrt{p^{2}-x^{2}}=p(x-1)\), and squaring gives \(x\left(x(p^{2}+1)-2p^{2}\right)=0\). Rejecting the trivial \(x=0\) leaves \(x=\dfrac{2p^{2}}{p^{2}+1}\).

derivations.reasoning: Multiplying by 2: (a-b)x^2-(a+b)x+2b=0. x=1 gives (a-b)-(a+b)+2b=0, so 1 is a root; the product of roots is 2b/(a-b). Sympy solve returns [1, 2b/(a-b)].
derivations.solution: Multiplying through by 2 clears the fractions: \((a-b)x^{2}-(a+b)x+2b=0\). Substituting \(x=1\) gives \((a-b)-(a+b)+2b=0\), so 1 is a root. The product of the roots is \(\dfrac{2b}{a-b}\), so the second root is \(\dfrac{2b}{a-b}\).

derivations.reasoning: x^2-1/x^2=(x-1/x)(x+1/x). (x+1/x)^2=(x-1/x)^2+4=8, and x>0 gives x+1/x=2sqrt2, so the value is 2*2sqrt2=4sqrt2. Sympy on the positive root x=1+sqrt2 returns 4sqrt2.
derivations.solution: Use the factorisation \(x^{2}-\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}=\left(x-\dfrac{1}{x}\right)\left(x+\dfrac{1}{x}\right)\). From \(\left(x+\dfrac{1}{x}\right)^{2}=\left(x-\dfrac{1}{x}\right)^{2}+4=8\) and \(x>0\) we get \(x+\dfrac{1}{x}=2\sqrt{2}\). The value is therefore \(2\times 2\sqrt{2}=4\sqrt{2}\).

derivations.reasoning: Sum of squared differences = 2(a^2+b^2+c^2)-2(ab+bc+ca) = 6 gives ab+bc+ca=26. Then (a+b+c)^2 = 29+2(26) = 81, so a+b+c = +/-9.
q=1/p, so p/q+q/p = p^2+1/p^2 = p^2+q^2. Rationalising, p=9-4sqrt5 and q=9+4sqrt5, so p^2+q^2 = (161-72sqrt5)+(161+72sqrt5) = 322. Sympy simplify returns 322.
derivations.solution: Rationalising gives \(p=9-4\sqrt{5}\) and \(q=9+4\sqrt{5}\), so \(q=\dfrac{1}{p}\) and the expression \(\dfrac{p}{q}+\dfrac{q}{p}\) is simply \(p^{2}+q^{2}\). Since \(p^{2}=161-72\sqrt{5}\) and \(q^{2}=161+72\sqrt{5}\), the surds cancel and the sum is 322.

derivations.reasoning: 25^10 = 95367431640625; the last three digits are 625, so the hundreds digit is 6 (5^k ends in 625 for every even k >= 4).
derivations.solution: Note that \((25)^{10}=5^{20}\), and the last three digits of powers of 5 settle into a pattern: \(5^{4}=625\), \(5^{5}\) ends in 125, \(5^{6}\) ends in 625, and every even power from the fourth onwards ends in 625. Since \(5^{20}=95{,}367{,}431{,}640{,}625\), the last three digits are 625 and the digit in the hundreds place is 6.

derivations.reasoning: N = 252k+3 since lcm(4,6,7,9)=252. 252*3+3=759 is 3-digit; 252*4+3=1011. Brute-force search from 1000 returns 1011.
derivations.solution: A number leaving remainder 3 on division by 4, 6, 7 and 9 has the form \(N=252k+3\), because \(\operatorname{lcm}(4,6,7,9)=252\). Taking \(k=3\) gives \(759\), which is still a three-digit number, while \(k=4\) gives \(1011\). That is the smallest four-digit number with the property.

derivations.reasoning: The nested radical L satisfies L^2 = 2+L, so L = 2 (the positive root; -1 is rejected). cosec(theta) = 2 gives sin(theta) = 1/2.
derivations.solution: Let \(L\) be the value of the infinite nested radical, so that \(L=\sqrt{2+L}\). Then \(L^{2}=L+2\), giving \(L=2\) once the negative root is rejected. Hence \(\operatorname{cosec}\theta=2\) and \(\sin\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}\).

derivations.reasoning: cos = 8sin-4; substituting into sin^2+cos^2=1 gives 65s^2-64s+15=0 with roots s=3/5 and s=5/13. In the first quadrant cos>0 is required: s=5/13 gives cos=-12/13 and is rejected; s=3/5 gives cos=4/5. So cosec = 5/3 (numeric solve confirms theta=0.6435 rad, cosec=1.6667).
derivations.solution: Substituting \(\cos\theta=8\sin\theta-4\) into \(\sin^{2}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta=1\) gives \(65\sin^{2}\theta-64\sin\theta+15=0\), whose roots are \(\sin\theta=\dfrac{3}{5}\) and \(\sin\theta=\dfrac{5}{13}\). The second is rejected because it forces \(\cos\theta=-\dfrac{12}{13}\), impossible for \(0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}\); the first gives \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{4}{5}\), which is admissible. Hence \(\operatorname{cosec}\theta=\dfrac{5}{3}\).

derivations.reasoning: sec^2 = 1+tan^2, so 2t = t^2-1, i.e. t^2-2t-1=0 and t = 1+sqrt2 (positive root, required for 0<theta<pi/2). cot = 1/(1+sqrt2) = sqrt2-1.
derivations.solution: Replace \(\sec^{2}\theta\) by \(1+\tan^{2}\theta\); the equation becomes \(2\tan\theta=\tan^{2}\theta-1\), i.e. \(t^{2}-2t-1=0\) with \(t=\tan\theta\). Its roots are \(t=1\pm\sqrt{2}\), and \(0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) forces the positive one, \(t=1+\sqrt{2}\). Hence \(\cot\theta=\dfrac{1}{1+\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{2}-1\).

derivations.reasoning: sqrt((1-sin)/(1+sin)) = (1-sin)/|cos| which equals (1-sin)/cos = sec-tan when cos>0, so the difference is 0. Checked numerically at 20, 40, 65 and 80 degrees (deliberately not at 45): residual ~1e-125 in all cases.
derivations.solution: Multiply inside the radical by \(1-\sin\theta\) top and bottom: \(\sqrt{\dfrac{1-\sin\theta}{1+\sin\theta}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{(1-\sin\theta)^{2}}{\cos^{2}\theta}}=\dfrac{1-\sin\theta}{\lvert\cos\theta\rvert}\). Where \(\cos\theta>0\) this is exactly \(\dfrac{1-\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=\sec\theta-\tan\theta\), so the difference is 0. Strictly the identity needs \(\cos\theta>0\); the stem does not restrict \(\theta\), but that is the intended range.

derivations.reasoning: The two acute angles sum to 90 degrees and differ by pi/12 rad = 15 degrees, so they are 52.5 and 37.5 degrees. Only 52.5 is offered.
derivations.solution: The two acute angles of a right-angled triangle add to \(90^\circ\), and \(\dfrac{\pi}{12}\) radian is \(15^\circ\). Solving \(x+y=90^\circ\) with \(x-y=15^\circ\) gives the angles \(52.5^\circ\) and \(37.5^\circ\), and of these only \(52.5^\circ\) appears among the choices.

derivations.reasoning: 998 + sqrt(x^2-18x+76) = 10^3 gives sqrt(...) = 2, so x^2-18x+72=0 with roots 6 and 12. (alpha-beta)^2 = 324-288 = 36.
derivations.solution: The equation gives \(998+\sqrt{x^{2}-18x+76}=10^{3}\), so the radical equals 2 and \(x^{2}-18x+72=0\). Its roots are 6 and 12, so \((\alpha-\beta)^{2}=(\alpha+\beta)^{2}-4\alpha\beta=324-288=36\).

derivations.reasoning: (x^2+y^2)^2 = x^4+y^4+2x^2y^2 = 16x^2y^2 so x^2+y^2 = 4xy, giving log(x^2+y^2) = log x + log y + 2log 2 (I). (x^2-y^2)^2 = 12x^2y^2 so |x^2-y^2| = 2sqrt3 xy, giving log = log x + log y + log 2 + 0.5 log 3 (II). Verified numerically at x=1, y=sqrt(7+4sqrt3): both identities hold to 1e-15.
derivations.solution: From \(x^{4}+y^{4}=14x^{2}y^{2}\) we get \((x^{2}+y^{2})^{2}=x^{4}+y^{4}+2x^{2}y^{2}=16x^{2}y^{2}\), so \(x^{2}+y^{2}=4xy\) and \(\log_{10}(x^{2}+y^{2})=\log_{10}x+\log_{10}y+2\log_{10}2\), which is the first statement. Similarly \((x^{2}-y^{2})^{2}=x^{4}+y^{4}-2x^{2}y^{2}=12x^{2}y^{2}\), so \(\lvert x^{2}-y^{2}\rvert=2\sqrt{3}\,xy\) and its logarithm is \(\log_{10}x+\log_{10}y+\log_{10}2+0.5\log_{10}3\), which is the second. Both statements are therefore correct.

derivations.reasoning: With A=3x+y and B=x+5y the expression is A^2+AB-20B^2=(A+5B)(A-4B) = 2(4x+13y) * -(x+19y). Sympy factor gives -2(x+19y)(4x+13y), so both listed binomials are factors.
derivations.solution: Put \(A=3x+y\) and \(B=x+5y\); the expression becomes \(A^{2}+AB-20B^{2}=(A+5B)(A-4B)\). Substituting back, \(A+5B=8x+26y=2(4x+13y)\) and \(A-4B=-(x+19y)\), so the expression equals \(-2(4x+13y)(x+19y)\). Both listed binomials are therefore factors.

derivations.reasoning: Each denominator term satisfies (x+y)/(x-y) = 2x/(x-y) - 1, so the denominator equals 2N - 3 + 3 = 2N where N is the numerator. The ratio is 1/2; sympy simplify confirms.
derivations.solution: Each denominator term can be rewritten as \(\dfrac{x+y}{x-y}=\dfrac{2x}{x-y}-1\), and likewise for the other two. The denominator is therefore \(2N-3+3=2N\), where \(N\) is the numerator. The required ratio is \(\dfrac{N}{2N}=\dfrac{1}{2}\).

derivations.reasoning: From m = p sin^2 a + q cos^2 a: sin^2 a = (m-q)/(p-q), cos^2 a = (p-m)/(p-q), so tan^2 a = (m-q)/(p-m). From n = q sin^2 b + p cos^2 b: tan^2 b = (p-n)/(n-q). The ratio is (m-q)(n-q)/[(m-p)(n-p)]; sympy gives ratio - optionC = 0 exactly, and numeric checks at three (alpha,beta) pairs match C and not D.
derivations.solution: From \(p\sin^{2}\alpha+q\cos^{2}\alpha=m\) we get \(\sin^{2}\alpha=\dfrac{m-q}{p-q}\) and \(\cos^{2}\alpha=\dfrac{p-m}{p-q}\), so \(\tan^{2}\alpha=\dfrac{m-q}{p-m}\). The same working on \(q\sin^{2}\beta+p\cos^{2}\beta=n\) gives \(\tan^{2}\beta=\dfrac{p-n}{n-q}\). Dividing, \(\left(\dfrac{\tan\alpha}{\tan\beta}\right)^{2}=\dfrac{(m-q)(n-q)}{(p-m)(p-n)}\), and since reversing the sign of both brackets in the denominator leaves the product unchanged this equals \(\dfrac{(m-q)(n-q)}{(m-p)(n-p)}\).

derivations.reasoning: If beta = 90 - alpha then sin^2 b = cos^2 a and cos^2 b = sin^2 a, so n = q cos^2 a + p sin^2 a = m. Hence m - n = 0. Numeric check at alpha = 0.3, 0.8, 1.2 rad gives m-n ~ 1e-16 while mn-1 and m+n are far from zero.
derivations.solution: Complementary angles mean \(\beta=90^\circ-\alpha\), so \(\sin^{2}\beta=\cos^{2}\alpha\) and \(\cos^{2}\beta=\sin^{2}\alpha\). Substituting into the second relation, \(n=q\cos^{2}\alpha+p\sin^{2}\alpha\), which is precisely \(m\). Hence \(m-n=0\).

derivations.reasoning: p = cosec - sin = cos^2/sin and q = sec - cos = sin^2/cos, so p sin + q cos = cos^2 + sin^2 = 1. Sympy simplify returns 1; numeric checks at 17, 33, 58, 71 degrees all give 1.000000000000.
derivations.solution: Simplify each quantity: \(p=\operatorname{cosec}\theta-\sin\theta=\dfrac{1-\sin^{2}\theta}{\sin\theta}=\dfrac{\cos^{2}\theta}{\sin\theta}\), and in the same way \(q=\sec\theta-\cos\theta=\dfrac{\sin^{2}\theta}{\cos\theta}\). Therefore \(p\sin\theta+q\cos\theta=\cos^{2}\theta+\sin^{2}\theta=1\).

derivations.reasoning: p^2q^2 = sin^2 cos^2 and the identity p^2q^2(p^2+q^2+3) = 1 holds. Sympy simplify returns 1 symbolically; numeric checks at 17, 33, 58 and 71 degrees (deliberately not 45) all give 1.000000000000.
derivations.solution: With \(p=\dfrac{\cos^{2}\theta}{\sin\theta}\) and \(q=\dfrac{\sin^{2}\theta}{\cos\theta}\), write \(k=\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta\); then \(p^{2}q^{2}=k\). Also \(p^{2}+q^{2}=\dfrac{\cos^{6}\theta+\sin^{6}\theta}{k}=\dfrac{1-3k}{k}\), using the identity \(\sin^{6}\theta+\cos^{6}\theta=1-3\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta\). Hence \(p^{2}q^{2}\left(p^{2}+q^{2}+3\right)=k\left(\dfrac{1-3k}{k}+3\right)=1\).

derivations.reasoning: sin a = (4sqrt2/3) sin b and cos a = (2sqrt3/9) cos b. Substituting in sin^2 a + cos^2 a = 1 gives (32/9)s + (4/27)(1-s) = 1 with s = sin^2 b, so s = 1/4. Then sin^2 a = 8/9, cos^2 a = 1/9 and tan^2 a = 8 (exact rationals; ratio checks reproduce 4sqrt2/3 and 2sqrt3/9).
From the same system sin^2 beta = 1/4 and cos^2 beta = 3/4, so tan^2 beta = 1/3 (exact).
derivations.solution: Squaring both given ratios and substituting into \(\sin^{2}\alpha+\cos^{2}\alpha=1\) gives \(\dfrac{32}{9}\sin^{2}\beta+\dfrac{4}{27}\cos^{2}\beta=1\). Replacing \(\cos^{2}\beta\) by \(1-\sin^{2}\beta\) reduces this to \(\sin^{2}\beta=\dfrac{1}{4}\). Then \(\cos^{2}\beta=\dfrac{3}{4}\), so \(\tan^{2}\beta=\dfrac{1}{3}\).
